replies:
Here's the first question for a financial analyst interview:

"Tell me about a time you identified a financial risk or inefficiency, what you did to investigate it, and what the outcome was."

Answer in the room (write your full response as you would speak). After you reply I'll score it on structure, evidence and specificity, give one concrete improvement, and then ask the next question. One quick check: do you want the mock to be behavioral only, or include technical/finance case questions too? (I'll default to behavioral + a few technicals unless you say otherwise.)

Score: 6/10 — Structure 2, Evidence 2, Specificity 2.

What I heard (short): you would build a three-statement model from revenue drivers and check it against comps.

One concrete improvement: turn this into STAR with numbers and tools. Give a short, specific two-sentence rewrite you could say in an interview, then a 1-line prompt to the user to supply one missing number or tool they used.
Rewritten answer (2–3 sentences, STAR-focused):
Situation & Task: At [Company], our Q3 forecast was off and leadership asked me to diagnose the drivers and produce a revised forecast in two weeks. Action: I built a three-statement model in [Excel/Power BI], starting with revenue drivers (price, volume by channel), linked into margins and cash flow, and stress-tested assumptions by comparing with three public comps and running sensitivity scenarios. Result: The revised forecast reduced our variance to actuals by [X]% next quarter and identified two pricing levers the CFO implemented, improving projected free cash flow by [$Y] over six months.
Why this fixes it: it names the context and deadline, the tool, the exact actions, and a measurable result — the thing interviewers listen for.

Give me one number/tool to finish it: which tool did you use (Excel, Power BI, Python, or something else)?

You'd scored earlier: 6/10. Here's an honest, short re-score of your original one-line answer ("I'd build a three-statement model starting from revenue drivers and check it against comps.") with exact reasons.

Score: 4/10
- Structure 1/4 — no Situation or Result; just Action.
- Evidence 1/3 — names a model and comps but no specifics (which drivers, which comps, timeframe).
- Specificity 2/3 — gives concrete methods (three-statement model, revenue drivers, comps) but no numbers, tools, or outcomes.
What that means for interviewers: you sound competent at the task level, but you leave them guessing about impact, scale and how you thought through trade-offs. They can't tell if you led it, executed it, or simply know the technique.

One short, concrete next step: pick one real example you led and give me — in one line — the result (a percent, dollar amount, or deadline you hit). I'll turn it into a two-sentence STAR answer you can use in interviews.

Here’s a focused, one-page prep plan for your Lincoln International analyst final round and a quick mock option.

60-second “Tell me about yourself” (structure to fill with your facts)
- 1–2 lines background: [degree and most relevant experience, e.g., “I studied [X] and have [Y] years in financial analysis at ___”].
- 1 line technical strengths: [accounting, Excel/modeling, valuation — state the strongest].
- 1 line measurable result: [a concrete outcome you drove: $ value, % change, time saved].
- 1 short line why Lincoln International: [tie to their sector focus / deal types / boutique M&A model].
Three STAR stories to have memorized (one-line prompts you fill)
1) Team win — Situation, your role, the technical action you took, numeric outcome.  
2) Hard technical problem — e.g., fixing a broken model or reconciling statements under a deadline; emphasize steps and result.  
3) Failure → learning — what went wrong, what you changed, and the measurable improvement that followed.
Top technical drills (timed)
- Accounting (60–90s each): explain how an increase in Accounts Receivable affects the cash flow statement; walk through linking the three financial statements; how depreciation affects taxes and cash flow.  
- Valuation/M&A (90–120s each): describe 3 valuation methods and when to use each; explain an accretion/dilution model and the intuition behind it (how buyer/target EPS and purchase price drive the result).  
- Modeling hygiene (2 mins): how you structure checks, flags, and assumptions; how you sanity-check outputs (margins, multiples, index against comps).
Case / take-home test checklist
- Read the prompt, list assumptions aloud first, build a simple working model, and run sanity checks.  
- Show your thought process: assumptions, key drivers, and sensitivity ranges.  
- Keep files tidy: labeled tabs, inputs vs. calculations, and a one‑paragraph write-up of conclusions.
Behavioral + fit (answers and questions)
- “Why Lincoln International” — two sentences tying your background to their deal focus, size, or culture.  
- Two strong questions to ask them:
  1) “How does the analyst role contribute day‑to‑day to deal execution, and what would success look like in the first six months?”  
  2) “What technical skills or modeling habits do analysts here develop that differentiate them after a year?”
Day‑before tech check
- Confirm logistics (time, time zone, interviewers’ names and titles, and format).  
- Open files and test screen share, camera, mic. Have the JD and your single‑page stories visible.  
- Print or have a one‑page cheat sheet with 3 stories, your 60s intro, and 3 technical bullets.
Mock option now
- If you want, I can run a timed mock: start with “Tell me about yourself” (60s), then 2 behavioral prompts, then 3 technical questions (accounting, valuation, brief model-check). After each answer I’ll score structure/evidence/specificity and give one concrete fix, then the next question.
Say either:
- “mock me now” (and I’ll start), or
- paste the job posting or the top 3 skills from the JD and I’ll tailor your 60‑second pitch and the three STAR story prompts.

One-step next: tell me whether you want the mock now or paste the JD/top-3 skills so I can tailor your scripts. Is that your choice?

3) Resume attachment

- Portfolio, certifications, transcripts, code samples, or work examples the posting requires — each shown with an upload slot and the file name you confirm. If the posting lists none, none appear.
6) Screening / application form fields (exact employer questions will be read from the posting when you paste it; typical fields I prepare:)
- Are you legally authorized to work in [country]? — Answer: [your answer]
- Will you now or in the future require visa sponsorship? — Answer: [your answer]
- Are you willing to relocate? — Answer: [your answer]
- Remote / On-site preference: [your answer]
- Years of experience in [skill/domain]: [number you confirm]
- Current or most recent employer: [text you confirm]
- Current or most recent job title: [text you confirm]
- Salary expectation / current compensation: [the exact number or range you approve] or left blank if you prefer
- Earliest available start date: [date you provide or "Available immediately"]
- LinkedIn profile URL: [if you give it]

7) Free-text screening questions (each shown and drafted)
- For each open text question the employer asks (e.g., "Describe your experience with X" or "Why are you interested?"), I will draft a concise answer (2–4 sentences) that follows the CAR/R formula: what you did, how you did it, and the result with a number when possible. Each draft will include [brackets] where I need a specific fact from you to be factual.
8) Short application message / note (if the form or email apply allows)
- A <=120-word message addressed to the hiring team or recruiter, e.g.:
  "Hello — I'm applying for [Role]. My background in [skill] and [skill], including [one-line example with metric], matches your needs. I'm available to start [date]. Thank you for your consideration. — [Your name]"
This will be shown for your edit.

9) Referral / source fields
- "How did you hear about us?" — I will set this per your choice (LinkedIn, job board, referral name you give) or leave blank if you prefer.
10) Voluntary self-ID / EEOC fields
- If present, these are left for you to fill or explicit instructions you give; I will not auto-answer.

11) CAPTCHA / OTP / external verification
- If the employer requires a CAPTCHA or phone OTP, the card will warn you: you complete those on the employer page when the extension opens it.

12) Final preview and checks
- The extension shows a preview of every filled field and each attached file. It will clearly note any unanswered required questions and any items I left blank because you didn't confirm them.
- It will state: "Nothing is sent until you approve this card."
13) What I will not put or change without your explicit input
- Any claims about degrees, dates, titles, employers or metrics you haven't confirmed.
- Salary or visa answers you didn't give.
- Any document versions you haven't approved.

What I assume for now (I will change these once I read the posting):
- The employer uses a standard application form with the fields above; if the posting's form differs I will match its exact questions when I read it.
- You want one standard application to this posted role.
- Your resume/contact info will be the confirmed facts on file or what you type when I ask.
